uncited: This family defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories used to approximate camera movement during shutter exposure time for motion blur synthesis.
It solves the problem of how to interpolate between known camera poses to generate intermediate virtual views.

The choice of representation is primarily driven by the complexity of the motion and the duration of the exposure: linear interpolation is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions.
All representations in this family operate within the Lie group SE(3) to ensure valid rigid body transformations.
The core mechanism involves optimizing a set of parameters to define the path between camera poses.
The optimization targets the camera poses themselves, rather than just the trajectory shape, allowing the model to adapt to the specific blur characteristics of the input data.
Linear interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by optimizing only the start pose $\mathbf{T}_{start}$ and the end pose $\mathbf{T}_{end}$.
The intermediate poses are generated by linearly interpolating between these two endpoints.
Cubic B-spline interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by jointly optimizing four control knots: $\mathbf{T}_1, \mathbf{T}_2, \mathbf{T}_3,$ and $\mathbf{T}_4$.
The authors conducted experiments on both synthetic datasets (Deblur-NeRF-S, MBA-VO) and real datasets (Deblur-NeRF) to assess the impact of trajectory representations.

They found that while linear interpolation performed comparably to cubic B-splines on synthetic data, the latter was necessary for real data to handle complex motions and longer exposure times effectively.
